vignette:
Imani speaks of her life in two distinct parts: before the windowless room, and after. Before, in her home country, she was a university student, studying political science. Her world was one of books, spirited debates in cafes, and articles she wrote for an underground student newspaper-articles that were sharp, hopeful, and dangerously critical of the ruling regime. She remembers the smell of jacaranda blossoms and roasted maize on the street. She remembers laughing with her friends, feeling that their words were small stones that could, with enough time, build a new foundation for their country.

The men who came for her arrived at dawn. They did not knock. The part of her story that follows is told in fragments, like shards of glass she is still afraid to touch. She speaks not of the specific acts, but of the sensory details that have become permanently etched into her memory. The abrasive feel of the burlap sack pulled over her head, the suffocating smell of damp concrete, the constant, low hum of a generator that seemed to burrow into her skull. For weeks, time was measured only by the scrape of a metal tray on the floor and the blinding glare of a single bulb being switched on. Her body was not her own, her voice was not her own. She learned that the most profound terror was not the pain, but the absolute loss of control, the feeling of being erased while still breathing.

When she was finally released, a skeletal ghost of herself, her family scraped together everything they had to get her out of the country. She arrived in a new city, a new continent, with nothing but a small bag and the humming generator still buzzing in her ears.

For years, survival was the only goal. She met Ade, a kind, steady man whose presence felt like an anchor. They married. She found a job as a train conductor. The work suited her at first. It was structured, predictable. There was a uniform, a schedule, a clear set of rules. She was in control of a powerful machine, moving hundreds of people safely from one point to another. The rhythmic clatter of the wheels on the track was a soothing, mechanical mantra. For a decade, she built a life in the 'after.' She was Imani, the train conductor. Imani, the wife. The student who wrote dangerous words was buried deep.

But the past does not stay buried. Slowly, insidiously, the train began to turn on her. The hiss of the pneumatic doors opening became the sharp intake of breath of the man in the room. The sudden darkness as the train plunged into a tunnel was the bag being pulled over her head again. The confined space of the conductor's cab, once a sanctuary of control, began to feel like a cell. She would stand at the controls, her knuckles white, her heart hammering against her ribs, convinced the walls were closing in.

She started seeing threats everywhere. A passenger arguing with another became a prelude to violence. She would scan the faces in the crowd on the platform, a cold dread coiling in her stomach, searching for a face she could not name but would never forget. At home, she became distant. Ade's gentle touch in the middle of the night would make her flinch, her body rigid with a terror her waking mind couldn't explain. He would pull back, his face a mask of hurt and confusion. She works overtime now, taking any shift she can get, because the motion of the train is better than the stillness of her own mind. The humming in her ears is louder than ever, a constant reminder that while she may have escaped the room, she never truly left.
